terms: Concept generation
Brainstorming, SCAMPER, mood boards and morphological charts produce divergent ideas; convergence selects strongest concept.
Design cycle stages
IBDP DT uses analysing, designing, planning, creating, evaluating; iterative loops repeat as understanding develops.
Double Diamond model
UK Design Council 2005 process: discover and define (problem), develop and deliver (solution); two divergent-convergent diamonds.
Inquiry and analysis
Identifies user needs through observation, interviews and PMI charts; benchmarks against existing solutions.
Prototyping iteration
Low-fidelity (paper, foam, cardboard) progresses through mid-fidelity (3D-printed) to high-fidelity working models; feedback drives refinement.
Specification document
Quantitative and qualitative criteria covering function, ergonomics, aesthetics, materials, cost, sustainability; agreed before design.
Computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM)
Using computers to control the whole production process, linking design data, manufacturing equipment, materials handling and quality systems together.
Just in case (JIC)
Holding buffer stocks of materials and finished goods to protect against demand surges or supply delays, at the cost of extra storage.
Just in time (JIT)
A production strategy where materials and components arrive only as they are needed, minimising the stock held and the cost of storage.
Lean production
An approach that aims to eliminate every form of waste, in time, materials, energy and effort, while still adding value for the customer.
Quality assurance (QA)
Building quality into every stage of the whole production system so that defects are prevented from occurring rather than detected afterwards.
Quality control (QC)
Inspecting and testing samples of output against set standards in order to detect and reject defective products after they are made.
Additive manufacturing
Techniques such as 3D printing that build a part layer by layer from digital data, adding material only where it is needed.
Batch production
Making a set quantity of identical products in groups, with the flexibility to switch the same equipment between different batches.
CNC machining
Computer numerical control machining, in which programmed machine tools cut material precisely and repeatably from digital design data.
Injection moulding
Forcing molten plastic into a closed mould under pressure, ideal for producing very large numbers of identical, accurate components.
Joining techniques
Permanent methods such as welding and adhesives, or temporary fastenings such as screws and bolts, used to assemble components into products.
Mass production
High-volume manufacture of standardised products on production lines, giving a low unit cost once the large set-up investment is recovered.
Moulding and casting
Shaping processes in which softened or liquid material is formed inside a mould or die, suited to producing many identical components.
One-off production
Making a single unique product to a client's exact requirements, typically using skilled labour and accepting a high cost per unit.
Robots in production
Reprogrammable machines used for repetitive, precise or hazardous manufacturing tasks, providing consistent quality and the ability to run continuously.
Scale of production
The volume strategy chosen for manufacture - one-off, batch, mass or continuous - each suiting different levels of demand and unit cost.
Subtractive manufacturing
Shaping techniques such as turning, milling and drilling that remove material from a larger solid block to leave the finished form.
Vacuum forming
Heating a thermoplastic sheet until soft, then drawing it down over a mould using suction to form thin shell-shaped products.
Anthropometric data
Statistical measurements of body dimensions; design typically accommodates 5th-95th percentile range; Henry Dreyfuss Designing for People 1955 set standards.
Cognitive ergonomics
Donald Norman's Design of Everyday Things 1988 covers affordances, signifiers, mappings, feedback; reduces user error through mental models.
Ergonomics scope
Discipline studying human-product interaction; HFES founded 1957; IEA 1959; covers physical, cognitive and organisational dimensions.
Fitts' Law 1954
Time to acquire target = a + b log2 (D/W + 1); models pointing tasks; informs touchscreen target sizing.
Reach envelope
Three-dimensional space accessible from a posture; primary, secondary and tertiary zones inform car cockpit and kitchen layouts.
Static vs dynamic anthropometrics
Static measures stationary body; dynamic captures reach, range of motion and clearance during movement.
Concept generation
Brainstorming, SCAMPER, mood boards and morphological charts produce divergent ideas; convergence selects strongest concept.
Design cycle stages
IBDP DT uses analysing, designing, planning, creating, evaluating; iterative loops repeat as understanding develops.
Double Diamond model
UK Design Council 2005 process: discover and define (problem), develop and deliver (solution); two divergent-convergent diamonds.
Inquiry and analysis
Identifies user needs through observation, interviews and PMI charts; benchmarks against existing solutions.
Prototyping iteration
Low-fidelity (paper, foam, cardboard) progresses through mid-fidelity (3D-printed) to high-fidelity working models; feedback drives refinement.
Specification document
Quantitative and qualitative criteria covering function, ergonomics, aesthetics, materials, cost, sustainability; agreed before design.
Brand
The identity of a company or product, including its name, values and visual style, which shapes consumer perception and loyalty.
Innovation
The successful commercial development and adoption of an invention, turning a new idea into a product that the market accepts.
Invention
A novel product, process or idea that did not exist before, often protected by a patent to stop others copying it.
Market pull
Product development driven by an identified consumer need or demand, where signals from the market determine what should be designed.
Market segmentation
Dividing a market into distinct groups of consumers who share characteristics such as age, income or lifestyle, so products can be targeted.
Technology push
Product development driven by new technology or materials, where research breakthroughs create products before clear consumer demand exists.
Computer-aided design (CAD)
Software used to create accurate virtual two-dimensional and three-dimensional models that can be modified, analysed and shared quickly and easily.
Conceptual modelling
Forming and refining ideas in the mind or as simple representations to explore how a design might work in principle.
Freehand sketching
Quick, informal drawings used early in designing to generate, explore and record many ideas rapidly and at very low cost.
Graphical modelling
Two-dimensional and three-dimensional drawings, such as sketches, perspective and orthographic views, used to develop and communicate design ideas.
Mock-up
A quick model, often full-scale and in cheap materials such as foam or card, used to assess the size, form and ergonomics of a design.
Model
A representation of a design idea - physical, graphical or virtual - used to explore, test and communicate the design before full production.
Orthographic projection
A formal working drawing showing accurate front, side and plan views with dimensions, so that a product can be manufactured correctly.
Physical modelling
A tangible three-dimensional model, often scaled or made in cheaper materials, used to test the form, proportion or function of a design.
Prototype
A working model close to the final product, used to test function, manufacturing methods and user response before committing to production.
Rapid prototyping
Producing physical parts directly from CAD data, for example by 3D printing, so that designs can be evaluated quickly.
Scale model
A physical model made proportionally smaller or larger than the real product, with every dimension reduced or enlarged by the same ratio.
Virtual prototyping
Testing a CAD model in software, for example simulating stresses, fit or movement, before any physical part is manufactured.
Clean technology
Production methods designed to prevent pollution and waste being created at source, rather than treating them after they have occurred.
Dematerialisation
Designing products and services to deliver the same function using less material and energy, for example through miniaturisation or digital delivery.
Design for disassembly
Designing products so they can be taken apart easily at end of life, enabling repair, reuse of components and recovery of materials.
Embodied energy
The total energy required to extract raw materials and then process, manufacture, package and transport a material or product.
Green design
Designing products to reduce environmental impact, for example by using fewer materials, less energy, and recyclable or low-impact components.
Life cycle analysis (LCA)
An assessment of a product's total environmental impact from raw material extraction through manufacture and use to its final disposal.
Non-renewable resource
A finite resource, such as crude oil or metal ore, that forms far more slowly than humans consume it and will eventually run out.
Recycling
Reprocessing waste material, for example melting down plastics or metals, into raw material for new products, reducing demand for virgin resources.
Renewable energy
Energy from naturally replenished sources such as solar, wind and hydro, used in production to reduce dependence on fossil fuels.
Renewable resource
A natural resource, such as timber or solar energy, that is replenished at a rate comparable to its consumption when managed responsibly.
Reserves
The portion of a resource that has already been discovered and can be extracted economically using current technology and prices.
Waste hierarchy
A ranking of waste strategies where reducing consumption is most effective, followed by reusing products, then recycling materials into new feedstock.
Cradle to cradle
William McDonough and Michael Braungart 2002 book; biological and technical nutrient cycles eliminate waste.
EU Ecodesign Directive
Directive 2009/125/EC sets minimum efficiency for energy-related products; banned filament bulbs in EU from 2012.
Eco-indicator 99
Pre 1999 single-score LCA method aggregating ecosystem quality, human health and resources damage; updated to ReCiPe 2008.
Embodied energy
Total energy used to produce a material; aluminium ~155 MJ/kg, steel ~30 MJ/kg, glass ~15 MJ/kg, virgin polymers ~80 MJ/kg.
Life Cycle Assessment
ISO 14040 (2006) standardises cradle-to-grave impact assessment; covers extraction, manufacture, transport, use, disposal.
Six Rs framework
Reduce, refuse, reuse, repair, recycle, rethink; design strategy for circular economy adoption.
Accessibility standards
WCAG 2.1 (W3C 2018) for digital; ADA 1990 US physical; ISO 21542 (2011) built environment guidance.
Empathy mapping
Dave Gray XPLANE 2005 visualises user thinks, says, feels, does; complements IDEO's Field Guide to Human-Centered Design 2015.
Inclusive design
Microsoft Inclusive Design Toolkit 2016 by Kat Holmes; solve for one, extend to many; permanent, temporary, situational disabilities.
Journey mapping
Visualises user touchpoints across time; identifies pain points and opportunities; service blueprint adds backstage processes.
Personas
Alan Cooper's About Face 1995 popularised personas; fictional users encode research; primary, secondary, anti-personas.
User-centred design
Donald Norman 1986 framed UCD in User Centered System Design; ISO 9241-210 (2010) sets standard process.
